notes.5: Route that bounces the user onward after login.
notes.7: Issues an HTTP redirect to whatever `next` contains.

options.label: A 302 redirect isn't cached, so the client makes an extra request
options.whyWrong: Caching behavior is irrelevant to the security issue.

options.label: `next` is attacker-controlled and used directly as the redirect target, so a link to this trusted site can bounce victims to an attacker's site (phishing)
`req.query.next` may be an array, causing a type error
options.whyWrong: A type edge case is a robustness nit, not the redirect abuse.

options.label: Block values starting with 'http://' or 'https://'
options.whyWrong: Protocol-relative `//evil.com` and backslash tricks like `/\evil.com` bypass this and still redirect off-site.

options.label: Allow only a site-relative path (a single leading slash, not '//')
encodeURIComponent(next) before redirecting
options.whyWrong: That corrupts a legitimate path and still can't confirm the destination is your site.

options.label: Check that next contains your domain name
options.whyWrong: `https://evil.com/?x=mysite.com` contains it; substring checks are trivially bypassed.

training.exploit: Send a victim `https://trusted-site/go?next=https://evil.example/login` — a link on the real domain that silently lands them on a look-alike login page to harvest credentials. `next=//evil.example` works too via protocol-relative URLs.

hints.line: Where does user input become the place the browser is sent?
hints.bugClass: The destination of a redirect is user-chosen.
hints.why: Who benefits from a link on your domain that lands elsewhere?
hints.fix: Permit only destinations within your own site.

writeup.summary: `res.redirect(next)` sends the browser wherever `next` says. Because the link lives on the trusted domain, attackers use it in phishing: victims trust the first URL and get bounced to a credential-stealing clone. Safe handling allows only site-relative paths (a single leading `/`, not `//`), or an explicit allowlist of destinations. Blocklisting `http://` misses protocol-relative and backslash forms.
